name: Cosmic impiety and the intoxication of power
plain_explanation: Russell worries that philosophies which make truth depend on human action, rather than on facts we cannot control, encourage a dangerous pride -- the feeling that humanity can remake reality itself to suit its wishes, with no limits imposed by 'stubborn facts.'
precise_definition: Russell's diagnosis of a broader intellectual and political danger: the traditional concept of 'truth' as dependent on facts largely outside human control has historically instilled a necessary humility in philosophy; when instrumentalism removes this check, it takes 'a further step... on the road towards a certain kind of madness -- the intoxication of power which invaded philosophy with Fichte,' a danger Russell calls the greatest of his time.
why_it_mattered: This is Russell's culminating criticism of instrumentalism, generalizing his technical objections into a warning about the social and political consequences of any philosophy of unlimited human power, whether individual (Nietzsche) or collective (Dewey).
historical_origin: Traced by Russell to Fichte as the point at which this 'intoxication' entered philosophy, and illustrated by the modern Italian pragmatist Papini's call to substitute the 'Imitation of God' for the 'Imitation of Christ.'
associated_philosopher: Bertrand Russell (as a critique of John Dewey and modern power-philosophies generally)
examples: The historical progression from Greek dread of hubris, through Christian humility before God, to Renaissance human pride, to modern technique's revival of 'the sense of the collective power of human communities.'
Papini's slogan urging the 'Imitation of God' in place of the 'Imitation of Christ.'
competing_positions: Dewey's own instrumentalism, which Russell treats not as consciously embracing this danger but as unintentionally contributing to it
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Explicitly framed by Russell in terms of humanity's changing religious and cultural relationship to a non-human universe, from Greek Necessity through Christian humility to modern technological pride.
